{{Short description|Concept in survival analysis}}
{{orphan|date=January 2018}}
In [[survival analysis]], hazard rate models are widely used to model duration data in a wide range
of disciplines, from bio-statistics to economics.<ref>{{Cite report|url=https://www.iser.essex.ac.uk/files/teaching/stephenj/ec968/pdfs/STB-39-pgmhaz.pdf|title=Estimation of discrete time (grouped duration data) proportional hazards models: pgmhaz|last=Jenkins|first=Stephen P|publisher=ESRC Research Centre on Micro-Social Change, University of Essex}}</ref>

Grouped duration data are widespread in many applications. Unemployment durations are typically measured over weeks or months and these time intervals may be considered too large for continuous approximations to hold. In this case, we will typically have grouping points <math>t_{a}</math>, where <math>a=1,...,A.</math>. Models allow for [[Time-invariant system|time-invariant]] and [[Time-variant system|time-variant]] [[Covariate|covariates]], but the latter require stronger assumptions in terms of [[exogeneity]].<ref>Wooldridge, J. (2002): Econometric Analysis of Cross Section and Panel Data, MIT Press, Cambridge, Mass.</ref>  The discrete-time hazard function can be written as:

<math>\lambda_{d}(t_{a}| \chi)= Pr(t_{a-1}\leqslant T <t_{a} |  T \geqslant t_{a-1},x[t_{a-1}])= \frac{S(t_{a-1} | \chi ) - S(t_{a} | \chi) }{S (t_{a-1}| \chi) }

</math>

where <math>S(t_{a}  |\chi)

</math> is the [[Survival function|survivor function]]. It can be shown that this can be rewritten as:

<math>\lambda_{d}(t_{a} | \chi) = 1-exp \biggl(-\int \lambda (s)  ds \biggr)= 1-exp  \Bigl(-exp (ln\lambda_{0s}+x (t_{s-1})'\beta)\biggl)

</math>

These probabilities provide the building blocks for setting up the [[Likelihood function]], which ends up being:<ref>Cameron A. C. and P. K. Trivedi (2005): Microeconometrics: Methods and Applications. Cambridge University Press, New York.</ref>

<math>L(\beta,\lambda) = \textstyle \prod[\prod exp(-exp(ln\lambda_{0s}+x_{i}(t_{s}-1)'\beta)\bigr)]\times \bigl(1-exp\bigl(-exp (ln\lambda0_{ai}+ x_{i}(t_{a-1})'\beta)\bigr)\Bigr)

</math>

This maximum likelihood maximization depends on the specification of the baseline hazard functions. These specifications include fully [[Parametric model|parametric models]], piece-wise-constant proportional hazard models, or partial likelihood approaches that estimate the baseline hazard as a nuisance function.<ref>Wooldridge, J. (2002): Econometric Analysis of Cross Section and Panel Data, MIT Press, Cambridge, Mass.</ref> Alternatively, one can be more flexible for the baseline hazard <math>\lambda^d_{0}(t)

</math> and impose more structure for  <math>\lambda^d_{i}(t)=\lambda^d_{0}(t)exp(-x_{i}'\beta).

</math> This approach performs well for certain measures and can approximate arbitrary hazard functions relatively well, while not imposing stringent computational requirements.<ref>Han, A. K., and J. A. Hausman (1990): Flexible Parametric Estimation of Duration and Competing Risk Models. Journal of Applied Econometrics, 5, pp. 1-28</ref>  When the covariates are omitted from the analysis, the maximum likelihood boils down to the [[Kaplan–Meier estimator|Kaplan-Meier estimator]] of the survivor function.<ref>Lancaster, T. (1990): The Econometric Analysis of Transition Data. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge.</ref>

Another way to model discrete duration data is to model transitions using [[binary choice model]]s.<ref>Cameron A. C. and P. K. Trivedi (2005): Microeconometrics: Methods and Applications. Cambridge University Press, New York.</ref>
